In this series, we will be using 3ds Max and later Unreal Engine for outputting a cinematic. The principles used here are also transferable to Maya, Blender, etc. To start with, a cage for the tint was built. The canvas will be attached underneath the poles. For the avatar in Marvelous Designer, the ground will need to be included for the canvas to rest on. The tint is built in four similar pieces and then sewn together where they are going to be attached. In the front of the tint, a heavier canvas will be needed that the character can push open. When it emerges from the tint, this will all be set up with the fabric settings. The canvas will be attached to the main center pole using these small straps attached to these rings. I was able to make one strap and then copy and paste the rest and sew them to the internal lines that line up to the rings. To get the wrinkles on the straps attaching the canvas to the poles, the straps were made longer than the internal lines where they are sewn. Before I move on, it is useful to set the UVs even though I will be editing them later in 3ds Max. Using the UV packing option will automatically layout UVs for you. It is fine that all UVs are on one UDIMM for this workflow. Once the tint canvas is built, I export it as an OBJ with the following settings. Thin, Unweld, and Single Object. The tint movement was simmed with a planar wind with 10,000 strength and 80 turbulence. As you can see, the tint fabric for the door is a heavier cloth and does not move as much. I have set the weight to 90, friction to 18 so it stays in place and thickness to 20. For the movement of the tint canvas in the wind, we will be using a point cache. 3ds Max uses the point cache too. For Maya you can use the Maya cache options. Make sure the export settings are the same as the settings used to export the OBJ. I always use Unweld and Thin as any thickness needed I will add later. Lastly, for this cable on the tint, I used an animated turntable to wind up the inner wires. Pin the top of the three fabric pieces that will make up the inner wire. Next, pin the bottoms of the pieces to the turntable. Record the simulation. Because I want this to be wound more, delete the garment animation at the end and scrub to the beginning of the sequence. Unattach the pins and reattach to the turntable. While it would have been easier to just use a twist modifier in 3ds Max, I like the more organic and random way this looks. The ropes that are holding the hanging bags were made in the same way. These ropes can be exported as thick. To position the cable, we will make a long thin pattern that will drive the finished cable. Pin the top and bottom of the pattern. Set the fabric to be leather. Position the cable where it should be attached using the pins and while the simulation is running. Set the fabric to be leather. Because the Marvelous Designer Groundplane is higher than the g.o. from the scene, I need to turn it off. Now I can do this with the Arduino处. Export an OBJ and name it Cable Simmed. Right-click in the 3D window and select Reset 3D Arrangement. Export another OBJ and name it Cable Flat. In 3ds Max, import both cable pieces and use the Morph modifier so the cable can move from flat to the simmed shape. Add a Shell modifier and make it around the thickness of the cylinder. Build a cylinder to fit around the flat cable. The coiled wire will fit inside the cylinder. Using Skin Wrap, wrap the cylinder to the cable piece. With Animate on, morph the cable from flat to the simmed shape. Export the cylinder which now deforms from flat state to simmed shape as an alembic. Back in Marvelous Designer, import the cylinder as an avatar. I will use the same cloth used for the cable animation and widen it so I can wrap it around the cylinder avatar. A quick way to do this is to select Pin and double-click on each long edge of the pattern. This will select the entire edge at once and then move the pin selection so it goes around the cylinder. Select the top of the pattern with pins and attach to the avatar. Record the simulation. Now we will fix the outer cable hose. I am using the Shrinkage Weft and Shrinkage Warp on the pattern to create a loose-fitting hose. Export as an OBJ. This concludes part 1 of this series. Thanks for watching. Please like and subscribe. See you in the next video.
summary: ```markdown # Cfx Workflow: Part 1 - Tent (Marvelous Designer + 3Ds Max) ## Introduction This video is a work of fiction. Any resemblance to actual persons, living or dead, is coincidental and unintentional. If you find the video useful, please like, share the video, and subscribe. Thanks for watching it. If you have any questions or other problems, please post them in the comments. ## Overview of the Series Welcome to the Marvelous Designer in CFX series. For Part 1, we will be looking at the tent used in the first shot. In this series, we will be using 3ds Max and later Unreal Engine for outputting a cinematic. The principles used here are also transferable to Maya, Blender, etc. ## Building the Tent To start with, a cage for the tent was built. The canvas will be attached underneath the poles. For the avatar in Marvelous Designer, the ground will need to be included for the canvas to rest on. The tent is built in four similar pieces and then sewn together where they are going to be attached. ### Canvas and Structure In the front of the tent, a heavier canvas will be needed that the character can push open. When it emerges from the tent, this will all be set up with the fabric settings. The canvas will be attached to the main center pole using small straps attached to rings. I was able to make one strap and then copy and paste the rest, sewing them to the internal lines that line up with the rings. ### Wrinkles and UV Layout To get the wrinkles on the straps attaching the canvas to the poles, the straps were made longer than the internal lines where they are sewn. Before I move on, it is useful to set the UVs even though I will be editing them later in 3ds Max. Using the UV packing option will automatically layout UVs for you. It is fine that all UVs are on one UDIMM for this workflow. ## Exporting the Tent Canvas Once the tent canvas is built, I export it as an OBJ with the following settings: Thin, Unweld, and Single Object. The tent movement was simulated with a planar wind with a strength of 10,000 and turbulence of 80. As you can see, the tent fabric for the door is a heavier cloth and does not move as much. I have set the weight to 90, friction to 18 so it stays in place, and thickness to 20. ## Point Cache and Animation For the movement of the tent canvas in the wind, we will be using a point cache. 3ds Max uses the point cache too. For Maya, you can use the Maya cache options. Make sure the export settings are the same as the settings used to export the OBJ. I always use Unweld and Thin, as any thickness needed I will add later. ## Cable Simulation Lastly, for this cable on the tent, I used an animated turntable to wind up the inner wires. Pin the top of the three fabric pieces that will make up the inner wire. Next, pin the bottoms of the pieces to the turntable and record the simulation. Because I want this to be wound more, delete the garment animation at the end and scrub to the beginning of the sequence. Unattach the pins and reattach them to the turntable. ### Organic Look vs. Twist Modifier While it would have been easier to just use a twist modifier in 3ds Max, I like the more organic and random way this looks. The ropes that are holding the hanging bags were made in the same way. These ropes can be exported as thick. ## Finalizing the Cable To position the cable, we will make a long thin pattern that will drive the finished cable. Pin the top and bottom of the pattern and set the fabric to be leather. Position the cable where it should be attached using the pins while the simulation is running. ### Exporting Cable Models Since the Marvelous Designer ground plane is higher than the geometry from the scene, I need to turn it off. I can do this with the Arduino. Export an OBJ and name it "Cable Simmed." Right-click in the 3D window and select "Reset 3D Arrangement." Export another OBJ and name it "Cable Flat." ## 3Ds Max Adjustments In 3ds Max, import both cable pieces and use the Morph modifier so the cable can move from flat to the simmed shape. Add a Shell modifier and make it around the thickness of the cylinder. Build a cylinder to fit around the flat cable. The coiled wire will fit inside the cylinder. Using Skin Wrap, wrap the cylinder to the cable piece. With Animate on, morph the cable from flat to the simmed shape. Export the cylinder, which now deforms from flat state to simmed shape as an Alembic. ## Importing Back to Marvelous Designer Back in Marvelous Designer, import the cylinder as an avatar. I will use the same cloth used for the cable animation and widen it so I can wrap it around the cylinder avatar. A quick way to do this is to select Pin and double-click on each long edge of the pattern. This will select the entire edge at once, and then move the pin selection so it goes around the cylinder. Select the top of the pattern with pins and attach it to the avatar. Record the simulation. ## Final Adjustments Now we will fix the outer cable hose. I am using the Shrinkage Weft and Shrinkage Warp on the pattern to create a loose-fitting hose. Export as an OBJ. ## Conclusion This concludes Part 1 of this series. Thanks for watching. Please like and subscribe. See you in the next video. ```
